tagline: Island of lemurs and upside-down trees
overview:
Madagascar is the fourth-largest island in the world, floating in the Indian Ocean about 400 kilometers off the southeast coast of Africa. It is roughly the size of Texas, or a little bigger than France. Because it split from Africa and India tens of millions of years ago, its plants and animals evolved on their own, and about 90 percent of its wildlife is found nowhere else on Earth, including all of the world's lemurs. The capital, Antananarivo, sprawls over hills in the central highlands, with red-brick houses stacked up steep slopes.

Around 30 million people live in Madagascar. Malagasy, a language whose closest relatives are spoken in Borneo, is the national language, and French is also official, reflecting the island's settlement from Asia and its colonial past. Most people are farmers, growing rice in terraced paddies and raising humped zebu cattle, and the island produces most of the world's natural vanilla. Madagascar is a republic with a president, and it is one of the poorest countries in the world despite its natural riches. Deforestation threatens its unique forests.
landAndNature: A spine of highlands runs down the island's length, dropping steeply to a narrow, rainy east coast of rainforest and gently to a drier west and a desert-like south. The Tsingy de Bemaraha is a forest of razor-sharp limestone needles, and the Avenue of the Baobabs is lined with trees 30 meters tall, their fat trunks storing water; baobabs are called upside-down trees because their bare branches look like roots. Madagascar's 100-plus species of lemurs range from the mouse lemur, small enough to fit in a hand, to the dancing sifaka and the ghostly aye-aye. Chameleons here include the world's largest and smallest, and the fossa, a cat-like predator, hunts lemurs. Coral reefs ring much of the coast, and humpback whales breed off Île Sainte-Marie each winter.
peopleAndCulture: The Malagasy descend from Austronesian sailors who arrived from Indonesia and from African settlers, and 18 main groups, such as the Merina of the highlands and the Sakalava of the west, share one language. Rice is eaten three times a day, often with romazava, a meat and greens broth, or ravitoto, pork with pounded cassava leaves. Respect for ancestors is central: the Merina hold famadihana, a joyful ceremony in which family remains are rewrapped in fresh silk and danced with, and fady, or taboos, guide daily behavior. Music features the valiha, a bamboo tube zither, and salegy dance rhythms. Rugby is surprisingly popular alongside soccer, and the Malagasy love the strategy board game fanorona. Lamba cloth is worn in bright wraps.
history: Madagascar was one of the last large landmasses settled by humans; Austronesian seafarers arrived around 1,500 years ago in outrigger canoes, later joined by Africans and Arab traders. Kingdoms rose along the coast, and in the late 1700s King Andrianampoinimerina began uniting the island under the Merina kingdom, which built a European-style state with schools and a written language. France conquered Madagascar in 1895 and exiled the last queen, Ranavalona III. A rebellion in 1947 was crushed with tens of thousands of deaths. Independence came on June 26, 1960. Since then the island has gone through socialist rule, protests, and several political crises, including a 2009 coup, with elections returning in 2013. Vanilla, mining, and tourism sustain a struggling economy.
funFacts: About 90 percent of Madagascar's animals and plants live nowhere else on Earth, including more than 100 kinds of lemur.
Madagascar grows most of the world's natural vanilla, whose flowers must be pollinated by hand.
The Malagasy language is most closely related to a language spoken in Borneo, 7,000 kilometers across the Indian Ocean.
Brookesia nana, a chameleon from northern Madagascar, is about the size of a sunflower seed, the smallest known reptile.
Baobab trees can store thousands of liters of water in their trunks and live for more than a thousand years.
